hook: At 16k tokens, one attention score matrix for one head is a gigabyte. The GPU is not slow. It is waiting on memory.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — At 16k tokens, one attention score matrix for one head is a gigabyte. The GPU is not slow. It is waiting on memory.

0:15 QUESTION — Every model you use, Llama 3, Claude, GPT, runs attention through FlashAttention or something like it. Before we write it, we have to prove the problem is real. Is naive attention compute-bound or memory-bound? Let's measure it instead of guessing.

1:00 INTUITION — Picture a chef with a tiny cutting board and a fridge across the room. Naive attention cooks S, writes it to the fridge, walks back, reads it, softmaxes it, writes it back, reads it again for PV. The cooking is fast. The walking is the job. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Shapes: Q, K, V are N by d. S = Q K^T / sqrt(d) is N by N. P = softmax(S) is N by N. O = P V is N by d. FLOPs: about 4 N^2 d for the two matmuls. HBM bytes for the naive version: read Q,K,V and write O is 4 N d elements, but S and P each get written and read, about 4 N^2 elements more. Arithmetic intensity of the softmax step alone is a handful of FLOPs per element, nowhere near the roughly 160 FLOPs per byte the 4090 needs to be compute-bound (165 TFLOPs over 1 TB/s). Memory for S at N=16384 in fp32: 16384^2 times 4 bytes = 1.07 GB, per head, per batch element.

5:00 CODE — Write naive_attention(q, k, v) with q,k,v shaped (B, H, N, d): s = q @ k.transpose(-2,-1) * d**-0.5, causal mask with torch.triu, p = s.softmax(-1), return p @ v. Then a sweep: for N in 512 to 16384, torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(), run forward, record torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() and time with CUDA events, 10 warmup, 50 reps. Same sweep for F.scaled_dot_product_attention.

8:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(naive_attention(q,k,v), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) in fp16. Then check the measured peak memory slope: naive grows 4x when N doubles, SDPA grows 2x. Predicted extra bytes for naive at N=8192, B=1, H=16, fp16: 16 times 8192^2 times 2 bytes, about 2.1 GB per N by N tensor.

9:30 MEASURE — Two log-log plots. Peak memory vs N: naive has slope 2, SDPA slope 1, naive OOMs on the 24 GB card somewhere past 16k with H=16. Time vs N: SDPA is several times faster at long N even though both do the same FLOPs. Annotate achieved TFLOPs for each.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — Attention did the same math both ways; the difference was HBM traffic for the N by N matrix. Interview line: standard attention is memory-bound because softmax is elementwise on an N squared matrix that lives in HBM.
11:45 NEXT — Next: Online softmax.
key_math: S = QK^T/sqrt(d) in R^{NxN}; FLOPs ~ 4N^2 d; naive HBM traffic ~ Theta(Nd + N^2); bytes(S) = N^2 * bytes_per_elem (16384^2 * 4 B = 1.07 GB)
code_task: naive_attention(q,k,v,causal=True) for q,k,v of shape (B,H,N,d); bench(fn, N_list) returning peak bytes via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated and ms via torch.cuda.Event timing; plots memory and time vs N for naive and F.scaled_dot_product_attention.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(naive_attention(q,k,v), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) in fp16; measured peak memory of naive minus SDPA within 10% of predicted B*H*N^2*2 bytes per materialized N x N tensor.
gotchas: Timing without torch.cuda.synchronize or CUDA events measures kernel launch, not the kernel; forgetting reset_peak_memory_stats between sizes so the peak sticks at the largest run; causal mask built as a fresh N x N bool tensor on every call adds its own memory to the measurement.
interview_q: Why is standard attention memory-bound even though it is mostly matmuls? Because it materializes the N x N score and probability matrices in HBM, and the softmax over them is elementwise with low arithmetic intensity, so runtime is dominated by reading and writing O(N^2) bytes rather than by FLOPs.
explainer: Here are Q, K and V, three thin tall matrices, N rows of d numbers each. They are small. They fit on the chip.
Multiply Q by K transpose and we get S, an N by N square. Watch it grow as N doubles. Four times the area every time.
The GPU has two memories. A tiny fast one on the chip, SRAM, and a huge slow one off the chip, HBM.
S is too big for SRAM, so it gets written out to HBM. That arrow is the expensive part.
Softmax reads S back in, does a few cheap operations per number, and writes P back out. More arrows, almost no math.
Then P is read in again to multiply with V. Three round trips for one N by N matrix.
On the roofline, softmax sits far left, below the slanted memory line. It is starved for bytes, not for compute.
So the fix is not faster math. The fix is never writing S to HBM at all.

Q times K^T animates into a square heatmap S; N doubles twice, square area quadruples, byte counter ticks 1 GB.
Chip diagram: small green SRAM box on die, large grey HBM box off die, bandwidth labels 1 TB/s vs ~20 TB/s on-chip.
S slides from SRAM to HBM along a thick red arrow labeled write N^2.
Red arrow back to SRAM, softmax glyph, red arrow out; FLOP counter barely moves while byte counter climbs.
P read back, multiplied with V, O emerges; tally shows 3 round trips of N^2.
Roofline plot, log-log; softmax point far left under the memory-bound slope, matmul point near the compute ceiling.
S fades out with a strike-through; caption 'never materialize S'.
short: The MEASURE beat: memory vs sequence length log-log plot, naive slope 2 crashing into the 24 GB line. Caption: 'Attention isn't slow. It's waiting on memory.'
yt_title: Why Attention Is Memory-Bound: measuring the N^2 wall on an RTX 4090
x_post: Naive attention and SDPA do the same FLOPs. At 8k tokens SDPA is several times faster and uses a fraction of the memory. The difference is one N x N matrix written to HBM and read back three times. Measured it on a 4090. Code + video:
linkedin: Started the FlashAttention module by measuring the problem instead of assuming it. Naive attention's peak memory grows with slope 2 on a log-log plot and OOMs a 24 GB RTX 4090 at long context, while PyTorch SDPA grows linearly. Same FLOPs, very different HBM traffic. The bottleneck is memory movement, not math.

hook: Softmax needs the max of the whole row before it can start. Except it doesn't. One rescale factor fixes that.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Softmax needs the max of the whole row before it can start. Except it doesn't. One rescale factor fixes that.

0:15 QUESTION — To never store the N by N matrix, FlashAttention has to softmax a row it only sees in chunks. Safe softmax looks like it needs three passes. This trick from Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018, is the whole reason FlashAttention is possible.

1:00 INTUITION — You are keeping a running total in dollars, then someone says from now on we count in a bigger currency. You do not restart. You multiply your total by the exchange rate and keep going. The running max is the currency. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Safe softmax: m = max_j x_j, l = sum_j exp(x_j - m), y_i = exp(x_i - m) / l. Three passes over x. Online: start m_0 = -inf, l_0 = 0. For each new x_j: m_j = max(m_{j-1}, x_j); l_j = l_{j-1} * exp(m_{j-1} - m_j) + exp(x_j - m_j). Why it is right: by induction l_{j-1} = sum_{i<j} exp(x_i - m_{j-1}); multiply by exp(m_{j-1} - m_j) and every term becomes exp(x_i - m_j). So l_N equals the safe-softmax denominator exactly. Block version: for a chunk with local max m_b and local sum l_b, m_new = max(m, m_b), l_new = l*exp(m - m_new) + l_b*exp(m_b - m_new). That merge is associative, which is what lets us split work later. Last step: the output. For attention we carry o too: o_new = o*exp(m - m_new) + sum_j exp(x_j - m_new) v_j. Divide by l at the end.

6:30 CODE — def online_softmax(x): loop over x[..., j], keep m and l tensors shaped x.shape[:-1], then one pass y = exp(x - m[...,None]) / l[...,None]. def online_softmax_blocked(x, block=64): same with chunks via x.split(block, -1), merge with the block formula. def merge(m1,l1,m2,l2) returns (m, l). Bonus: online_softmax_weighted_sum(x, v) that returns softmax(x) @ v in one pass, carrying o shaped (..., d). This is FlashAttention's inner loop in 15 lines.

9:30 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(online_softmax(x), torch.softmax(x, -1)) for x = torch.randn(4, 1000) * 30 in float32. Same for the blocked version with block sizes 1, 7, 64, 1000. torch.testing.assert_close(online_softmax_weighted_sum(x, v), torch.softmax(x,-1) @ v). Then the stress test: x * 1000, naive exp overflows to inf, ours stays finite and still matches.
11:00 MEASURE — Show HBM reads per element: naive softmax 3 reads 1 write, online 2 reads 1 write, fused with V 1 read. Print max abs error vs torch.softmax across block sizes, all around 1e-7.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — When the max changes, multiply the old sum by exp(m_old - m_new) and keep going. Interview line: online softmax makes the normalizer a mergeable, associative statistic, so softmax can be computed blockwise without seeing the whole row.
12:45 NEXT — Next: FlashAttention forward on paper.
key_math: m_j = max(m_{j-1}, x_j); l_j = l_{j-1} * exp(m_{j-1} - m_j) + exp(x_j - m_j); merge: m = max(m_a, m_b), l = l_a e^{m_a - m} + l_b e^{m_b - m}; o_new = o e^{m_old - m_new} + sum_j e^{x_j - m_new} v_j, y = o / l
code_task: online_softmax(x: (..., N)) -> (..., N); online_softmax_blocked(x, block); merge(m1,l1,m2,l2) -> (m,l); online_softmax_weighted_sum(x: (..., N), v: (N, d)) -> (..., d) computing softmax(x) @ v in one pass.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(online_softmax_blocked(x, b), torch.softmax(x, -1)) for b in [1,7,64,1000]; torch.testing.assert_close(online_softmax_weighted_sum(x, v), torch.softmax(x, -1) @ v); with x scaled by 1000 the result stays finite.
gotchas: Initializing m to 0 instead of -inf breaks rows that are all very negative; rescaling the new term but forgetting to rescale the old sum l; fully masked rows give m = -inf and exp(-inf - -inf) = nan, so guard with a where.
interview_q: How can you compute softmax in a single pass when you need the max for numerical stability? Track a running max m and a running sum l; whenever the max increases, rescale l by exp(m_old - m_new). The final l equals the stable denominator exactly, and the same rescale applies to a running weighted sum of V.
explainer: Here is one row of attention scores, a strip of numbers we will read left to right, one chunk at a time.
Safe softmax wants the biggest number first. That means reading the whole strip before doing anything. Three passes.
Instead we keep two numbers as we go. The biggest score so far, m, and a running sum, l.
New chunk arrives with a bigger score. Our old sum was measured against the old max, so it is now wrong.
Fix it with one multiply. Scale the old sum by e to the old max minus the new max. Every old term lines up.
Add the new chunk's terms, measured against the new max, and we are back in sync.
Two chunks processed by different workers can be merged with the same rule. Order does not matter.
Carry a running output alongside, rescaled the same way, and softmax times V happens in one pass.

Three arrows sweeping the full strip labeled pass 1 max, pass 2 sum, pass 3 normalize.
Two registers drawn as boxes, m and l, updating as the cursor moves.
A tall cell in chunk 3; m jumps; l box flashes red with a question mark.
l multiplied by exp(m_old - m_new) shown as a shrinking factor; bars inside l rescale.
New chunk bars added to l; l turns green.
Two strips processed in parallel, their (m,l) pairs merging into one via the merge formula.
Third register o (a small vector) rescaling in lockstep; final o / l equals softmax @ V.
short: The INTUITION + MATH rescale step: old sum times exp(m_old - m_new). Caption: 'The one line that makes FlashAttention possible.'
yt_title: Online Softmax from Scratch: the trick behind FlashAttention

linkedin: Implemented online softmax and its blockwise merge, then extended it to compute softmax(x) @ V in a single pass. It matches torch.softmax to ~1e-7 for every block size and stays finite when naive exp overflows. The key insight: the softmax normalizer is a mergeable statistic once you carry the running max.

hook: FlashAttention is not an approximation. It is the exact same attention, computed in tiles that never leave the chip.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — FlashAttention is not an approximation. It is the exact same attention, computed in tiles that never leave the chip.

0:15 QUESTION — Dao et al. 2022 got a 3x speedup on GPT-2 training and exact outputs. How do you compute softmax(QK^T)V without ever holding a full row of QK^T? We derive the update rule on a whiteboard before touching code.

1:00 INTUITION — Take a block of query rows and keep it on chip. Stream key and value blocks past it like a conveyor belt. For each block, compute a small tile of scores, fold it into a running output using online softmax, throw the tile away. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Split Q into T_r blocks of B_r rows, K and V into T_c blocks of B_c rows. For query block i, init O_i = 0 (B_r x d), m_i = -inf, l_i = 0 (B_r). For each j: S_ij = Q_i K_j^T / sqrt(d), shape B_r x B_c. m_ij = rowmax(S_ij). P~_ij = exp(S_ij - m_ij). l_ij = rowsum(P~_ij). m_new = max(m_i, m_ij). l_new = e^{m_i - m_new} l_i + e^{m_ij - m_new} l_ij. FA1 form: O_i = diag(l_new)^{-1} ( diag(l_i) e^{m_i - m_new} O_i + e^{m_ij - m_new} P~_ij V_j ). Then m_i = m_new, l_i = l_new. Proof sketch: at every step O_i equals the exact softmax of the columns seen so far times V; it is the online softmax from last episode with a vector numerator. FA2 simplification: keep O unnormalized, rescale by e^{m_i - m_new} only, divide by l once at the end. Save L_i = m_i + log l_i for backward. Block sizes: SRAM M bytes forces B_c = ceil(M/4d), B_r = min(B_c, d). HBM accesses drop from Theta(Nd + N^2) to Theta(N^2 d^2 / M).

7:30 CODE — Paper-faithful numpy-style sketch in a notebook cell: two nested Python loops over i and j with the exact update above, on N=8, d=4, B_r=B_c=2, printing O_i after each j so you can watch it converge. Keep it scalar and readable. Next episode turns it into a real PyTorch reference.

9:30 RECEIPT — np.testing.assert_allclose(fa1_paper(Q,K,V,Br=2,Bc=2), softmax(Q@K.T/np.sqrt(d)) @ V, rtol=1e-6) for N=8, then N=37 with ragged last blocks. Also assert the saved L equals logsumexp(S, axis=-1).
10:30 MEASURE — Table of HBM bytes moved for N=4096, d=64, M=100 KB shared memory on a 4090 SM: naive vs the Theta(N^2 d^2 / M) bound. Show the ratio, roughly an order of magnitude fewer bytes.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Outer loop holds Q on chip, inner loop streams K and V, online softmax glues the tiles together exactly. Interview line: FlashAttention is IO-aware exact attention; it trades a little recomputation and rescaling for never materializing the N by N matrix in HBM.
12:15 NEXT — Next: FlashAttention forward in PyTorch.
key_math: S_ij = Q_i K_j^T / sqrt(d); m_new = max(m_i, rowmax S_ij); l_new = e^{m_i - m_new} l_i + rowsum(e^{S_ij - m_new}); O_i <- e^{m_i - m_new} O_i + e^{S_ij - m_new} V_j (FA2, divide by l at end); L_i = m_i + log l_i
code_task: fa1_paper(Q, K, V, Br, Bc) in numpy: Q,K,V (N, d); loops over query blocks i and key blocks j; returns O (N, d) and L (N,). Prints intermediate O_i to show convergence.
receipt: np.testing.assert_allclose(O, softmax(Q@K.T/sqrt(d)) @ V, rtol=1e-6) for N in {8, 37}; np.testing.assert_allclose(L, logsumexp(Q@K.T/sqrt(d), -1)).
gotchas: Rescaling O by the new max but forgetting the l_i/l_new factor in the FA1 form, which double-normalizes; ragged final block when N is not a multiple of B_c silently reads garbage unless masked; mixing up which loop is outer (FA1 paper has K/V outer, FA2 swaps to Q outer, both are exact).
interview_q: Walk me through the FlashAttention forward. Tile Q into blocks kept in SRAM, stream K and V blocks, compute a B_r x B_c score tile, update a running max, running sum and unnormalized output with online softmax rescaling, and write only O and the logsumexp L to HBM. Output is exact.
explainer: Here is the full attention picture, the big N by N score square we refused to store last time.
Cut Q into horizontal strips and K and V into strips too. One strip of Q moves onto the chip and stays.
The first K strip slides in. Q strip times K strip gives a small tile of scores, just B r by B c.
We softmax the tile with its own max and multiply by the V strip. That is a partial answer.
Next K and V strip arrives. If its max is bigger, we shrink the old partial answer by e to the old max minus new max.
Add the new contribution. The running output now equals exact attention over everything seen so far.
After the last strip, divide by the running sum once. Write O to memory. The tiles never left the chip.
We also save one number per row, the log sum exp, so the backward pass can rebuild any tile later.

hook: Before you write a single Triton line, build a tiled FlashAttention in plain PyTorch you can step through with a debugger.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Before you write a single Triton line, build a tiled FlashAttention in plain PyTorch you can step through with a debugger.

0:15 QUESTION — Kernel bugs are silent. A wrong mask or a missed rescale gives numbers that look fine. Every serious kernel project, including FlashAttention itself, has a slow reference implementation. This one becomes the oracle for P1, feather-attn.

1:00 INTUITION — Same algorithm as the whiteboard, but batched over heads and with real tensor shapes. Loops over blocks stay as Python loops so you can print any tile. Speed is not the goal. Being obviously correct is. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Recap the FA2 forward we implement: for each Q block, O_acc = 0, m = -inf, l = 0. Per K block: S = Q_i K_j^T * scale; apply causal mask where col > row set -inf; m_new = max(m, S.amax(-1)); alpha = exp(m - m_new); P = exp(S - m_new[...,None]); l = alpha*l + P.sum(-1); O_acc = alpha[...,None]*O_acc + P @ V_j; m = m_new. End: O_i = O_acc / l[...,None], L_i = m + log(l). Causal skip: for block j entirely above the diagonal, j*B_c > (i+1)*B_r - 1, skip it. That saves about half the FLOPs.

4:30 CODE — def flash_fwd_ref(q, k, v, causal=False, Br=64, Bc=64) with q,k,v (B, H, N, d) returning (o, lse) with o (B,H,N,d), lse (B,H,N) in fp32. Loop i over range(0, N, Br), j over range(0, N, Bc). Use offsets row_idx = i + arange(Br), col_idx = j + arange(Bc) to build the causal mask per tile, and slice so ragged ends work. Accumulate in float32 even when inputs are fp16. Add a GQA path: k,v shaped (B, H_kv, N, d) and index head h // (H // H_kv).

8:30 RECEIPT — for causal in [False, True], N in [128, 257, 1000], d in [64, 128]: torch.testing.assert_close(flash_fwd_ref(q,k,v,causal)[0], F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=causal), atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5) in float32, and atol=2e-3 in fp16. Also torch.testing.assert_close(lse, torch.logsumexp(scores, -1)). GQA: compare against SDPA with enable_gqa=True.

10:30 MEASURE — Peak memory of flash_fwd_ref vs naive at N=8192 on the Mac: flat in N for the reference (only Br x Bc tiles), quadratic for naive. Time is terrible, and say so; that is the next episode's job.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — A slow, obviously-correct reference is the first deliverable of any kernel project. Interview line: I validate kernels against a tiled reference and against SDPA across ragged lengths, causal, GQA and dtypes, because the bugs hide at block boundaries.
12:15 NEXT — Next: FlashAttention forward in Triton.
key_math: alpha = exp(m - m_new); O_acc <- alpha O_acc + exp(S - m_new) V_j; l <- alpha l + rowsum(exp(S - m_new)); O = O_acc / l; lse = m + log l; skip block j if j*B_c > (i+1)*B_r - 1 (causal)
code_task: flash_fwd_ref(q, k, v, causal=False, Br=64, Bc=64) -> (o, lse); q (B,H,N,d), k,v (B,H_kv,N,d) for GQA; fp32 accumulators; ragged last blocks; causal block skipping.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(flash_fwd_ref(q,k,v,causal)[0], F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=causal, enable_gqa=True)) over N in {128,257,1000}, d in {64,128}, causal in {False,True}; lse matches torch.logsumexp(q@k.transpose(-2,-1)*scale masked, -1).
gotchas: SDPA's is_causal aligns the mask to the top-left, so with different query and key lengths your mask must match that convention; accumulating P @ V in fp16 drifts badly at long N, keep fp32 accumulators; scale must be d**-0.5 of the head dim, not of the model dim.
interview_q: How do you test a custom attention kernel? Build a simple tiled reference and compare both to SDPA in fp32 and the target dtype, sweeping ragged sequence lengths, causal and non-causal, GQA ratios and head dims, and also check the saved logsumexp, since block-boundary bugs only show up off the happy path.
explainer: Here is our batch of attention, four dimensions: batch, heads, sequence, head dim. We will tile only the sequence axis.
One Q block of 64 rows is picked out. Its accumulators start empty: output zeros, max minus infinity, sum zero.
A K block arrives. We compute its 64 by 64 score tile and paint the causal mask over the upper triangle.
Blocks entirely above the diagonal never get computed at all. Half the grid simply goes dark.
Inside each tile the same three updates run: new max, rescale factor alpha, then add P times V.
The last block is ragged, only 17 rows. Slicing handles it, and this is where most bugs live.
For grouped query attention, eight query heads share one key head. We just point them at the same K and V.
Finally we compare every output against PyTorch's SDPA. Green across the whole sweep means we have an oracle.

hook: About 120 lines of Triton, and your attention kernel runs within striking distance of PyTorch's built-in on a 4090.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — About 120 lines of Triton, and your attention kernel runs within striking distance of PyTorch's built-in on a 4090.

0:15 QUESTION — The reference is correct and slow. Now it becomes a real kernel: one program per Q block per head, K and V streamed through SRAM, tensor cores doing the matmuls. This is the forward half of P1, feather-attn.

1:00 INTUITION — The grid is a sheet of workers. Each worker owns 128 query rows of one head. It loops over K and V blocks, keeping its accumulator in registers. Nothing N by N ever exists anywhere. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Same update as before, now with exp2 for speed: precompute qk_scale = sm_scale * log2(e) = sm_scale * 1.44269504. Then p = exp2(s*qk_scale - m), alpha = exp2(m_old - m_new), and lse stored as m/log2(e) + log(l) so backward uses natural log. FLOPs for the TFLOPs number: forward = 4 * B * H * N^2 * d, halve it for causal. Roofline check: per Q block, arithmetic intensity grows with B_r, so bigger blocks mean more reuse of each K,V load.

4:00 CODE — @triton.jit def _attn_fwd(Q, K, V, O, LSE, stride_qb, stride_qh, stride_qn, stride_qd, ..., N, HEAD_DIM: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, CAUSAL: tl.constexpr). pid_m = tl.program_id(0), pid_bh = tl.program_id(1). Load q tile once with tl.load and a mask on rows < N. Loop start_n in range(0, hi, BLOCK_N): k = tl.load(...), s = tl.dot(q, tl.trans(k)), causal: tl.where(offs_m[:,None] >= offs_n[None,:], s, -inf); m_new = tl.maximum(m, tl.max(s,1)*qk_scale); p = tl.math.exp2(s*qk_scale - m_new[:,None]); alpha = tl.math.exp2(m - m_new); acc = acc*alpha[:,None] + tl.dot(p.to(v.dtype), v); l = l*alpha + tl.sum(p,1). Store acc / l[:,None] and lse. Python wrapper flash_fwd(q,k,v,causal) with grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK_M), B*H) and a @triton.autotune over BLOCK_M in {64,128}, BLOCK_N in {32,64}, num_warps {4,8}, num_stages {2,3}.

8:30 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(flash_fwd(q,k,v,causal), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=causal), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) in fp16 and bf16 for N in {128, 1000, 4096}, d in {64, 128}; also assert_close(lse, flash_fwd_ref(...)[1], atol=1e-3). Benchmark with triton.testing.do_bench.

10:30 MEASURE — TFLOPs/s vs N, causal and non-causal, d=64 and 128, fp16, B*H=32: yours, SDPA (which dispatches to the FlashAttention-2 backend on the 4090), naive. Report your percent of SDPA at N=4096. Expect the Triton-tutorial-level kernel to land in the same ballpark as SDPA, not above it.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — One program per Q block, K and V streamed, accumulators in registers, exp2 instead of exp. Interview line: the forward kernel is a loop of two tensor-core matmuls with an online-softmax rescale in between, and block sizes trade SRAM capacity against reuse.
12:45 NEXT — Next: The backward pass and recomputation.
key_math: qk_scale = sm_scale * log2(e); p = 2^{s*qk_scale - m}; alpha = 2^{m_old - m_new}; lse = m ln2 + ln l; FLOPs_fwd = 4 B H N^2 d (x0.5 causal); TFLOPs/s = FLOPs / time
code_task: Triton kernel _attn_fwd(Q,K,V,O,LSE, strides..., N, HEAD_DIM, BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, CAUSAL) with grid (cdiv(N,BLOCK_M), B*H); wrapper flash_fwd(q,k,v,causal) -> (o (B,H,N,d), lse (B,H,N) fp32); autotune configs; benchmark harness with triton.testing.do_bench.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(flash_fwd(q,k,v,causal)[0], F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=causal), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) for fp16/bf16, N in {128,1000,4096}, d in {64,128}; TFLOPs/s chart vs SDPA.
gotchas: Passing p in fp32 into tl.dot with fp16 v forces a slow path or a type error, cast p to v.dtype; forgetting masks on the ragged last K block so out-of-range keys get score 0 instead of -inf; mixing natural-log lse with exp2 in backward gives gradients off by a constant factor.
interview_q: Why does FlashAttention use exp2 and what limits its block size? exp2 maps to a single fast hardware instruction, so the softmax scale is folded with log2(e); block size is limited by shared memory and registers, since bigger Q and K tiles increase reuse and arithmetic intensity but reduce occupancy and can spill.
explainer: Here is the launch grid. Each square is one Triton program, owning one block of queries for one head.
Zoom into one program. Its query tile loads once from HBM into registers and stays for the whole loop.
Key and value tiles stream in one after another, double buffered so the next load overlaps this compute.
Q times K transpose runs on tensor cores. A small score tile appears, never leaving the chip.
We use exp base two, with the softmax scale pre-multiplied by log two of e. Same math, faster instruction.
Rescale the accumulator by alpha, add P times V, also on tensor cores. Update the running sum.
For causal attention, programs near the top stop early. Their loop is shorter. Work is uneven but halved.
At the end each program writes its output tile and one logsumexp per row. That is the entire HBM write.

hook: The FlashAttention backward stores less than the forward, and it is faster because of it. It recomputes P instead of saving it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The FlashAttention backward stores less than the forward, and it is faster because of it. It recomputes P instead of saving it.

0:15 QUESTION — Training needs dQ, dK, dV. Standard autograd would save the N by N matrix P, which is exactly what we refused to store. The fix is recomputation plus one clever scalar per row, D = rowsum(dO * O). This completes P1, feather-attn.

1:00 INTUITION — Saving P costs N squared memory and N squared HBM reads. Recomputing a tile of P from Q, K and the saved logsumexp costs one matmul on chip. On a GPU, FLOPs are cheap and bytes are expensive, so recomputing wins. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Forward: S = QK^T * c, P = softmax(S), O = PV, c = 1/sqrt(d). Backward from dO (N x d). Step 1: dV = P^T dO, because O is linear in V. Step 2: dP = dO V^T, shape N x N. Step 3, softmax Jacobian per row: dS_ij = P_ij (dP_ij - sum_k P_ik dP_ik). Step 4, the trick: sum_k P_ik dP_ik = sum_k P_ik sum_t dO_it V_kt = sum_t dO_it O_it = D_i. So D = rowsum(dO * O), an N-vector computed once from O and dO, no N by N anything. So dS = P * (dP - D[:,None]). Step 5: dQ = c * dS K, dK = c * dS^T Q. Recompute: P_ij = exp(S_ij - L_i) using the saved L = logsumexp. Memory saved for backward: Q, K, V, O, L. That is O(N d), not O(N^2).

6:00 CODE — Kernel 1, _attn_bwd_preprocess: D = (o.float() * do.float()).sum(-1), shape (B,H,N). Kernel 2, _attn_bwd_dkdv: grid over K blocks; each program loads K_j, V_j, loops over Q blocks i: recompute s = q @ k^T, p = exp2(s*qk_scale - lse_i*log2e), dv += p^T @ do, dp = do @ v^T, ds = p * (dp - D_i[:,None]), dk += ds^T @ q * sm_scale. Kernel 3, _attn_bwd_dq: grid over Q blocks; loop over K blocks, same recompute, dq += ds @ k * sm_scale. Splitting dq from dk/dv avoids atomics (FA2 style). Wrap all in class FlashAttnFn(torch.autograd.Function) with forward saving q,k,v,o,lse via ctx.save_for_backward.

9:30 RECEIPT — Two receipts. First, exactness of the math: wrap flash_fwd_ref plus a PyTorch tiled backward in a torch.autograd.Function and run torch.autograd.gradcheck(FlashRefFn.apply, (q,k,v), eps=1e-6, atol=1e-4) in float64 on small shapes (B=1,H=2,N=37,d=16). Second, the Triton kernel: compare dq, dk, dv against F.scaled_dot_product_attention(...).backward(do) using the FlashAttention repo's rule: max error of yours vs an fp32 reference must be no more than 2x the error of SDPA in the same dtype vs that fp32 reference.
11:30 MEASURE — Peak memory for forward plus backward at N=8192: naive autograd vs yours vs SDPA. Backward TFLOPs/s (backward FLOPs = 2.5x forward: 10 B H N^2 d counting recompute) vs SDPA.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — Save Q, K, V, O and logsumexp, recompute P per tile, and use D = rowsum(dO * O) to make the softmax backward local. Interview line: FlashAttention's backward avoids storing P by recomputing it from the logsumexp, and the softmax Jacobian collapses to P times (dP minus rowsum of dO times O).
13:15 NEXT — Next: FlashAttention 2 and 3.
key_math: dV = P^T dO; dP = dO V^T; D_i = sum_k P_ik dP_ik = rowsum(dO * O)_i; dS = P * (dP - D); dQ = c dS K; dK = c dS^T Q; recompute P_ij = exp(S_ij - L_i)
code_task: Triton kernels _attn_bwd_preprocess (D (B,H,N)), _attn_bwd_dkdv (grid over K blocks, accumulates dk, dv (B,H,N,d)), _attn_bwd_dq (grid over Q blocks); torch.autograd.Function FlashAttnFn with forward saving (q,k,v,o,lse); a float64 PyTorch tiled reference FlashRefFn for gradcheck.
receipt: torch.autograd.gradcheck(FlashRefFn.apply, (q,k,v), eps=1e-6, atol=1e-4) in float64; for the Triton kernel, (dq_yours - dq_fp32ref).abs().max() <= 2 * (dq_sdpa_fp16 - dq_fp32ref).abs().max(), same for dk and dv, causal and non-causal.
gotchas: gradcheck in fp32 or fp16 fails for numerical reasons, it must be float64 and small shapes; computing D from the fp16 O and dO without casting to fp32 loses precision at long N; forgetting the sm_scale on dK or dQ, or applying it twice because it was already folded into qk_scale.
interview_q: Derive the FlashAttention backward and explain why D = rowsum(dO * O) appears. The softmax Jacobian needs sum_k P_ik dP_ik per row; substituting dP = dO V^T gives sum_t dO_it (PV)_it = rowsum(dO * O)_i, so the correction is an N-vector computable from saved O, and P itself is recomputed tile by tile from the logsumexp.
explainer: Here is the forward we saved: Q, K, V, the output O, and one logsumexp per row. Notice what is missing. P.
The gradient dO flows in from the loss. First, dV is P transpose times dO. Simple, because O is linear in V.
Next, dP is dO times V transpose. Now we need the softmax backward, and that looks like it needs whole rows of P.
The softmax Jacobian subtracts, per row, the sum of P times dP. Watch that sum rearrange itself.
P times dO times V transpose regroups into dO times P V. And P V is just O, which we saved.
So the correction is D, the row sum of dO times O. One number per row, computed before any tiles.
Inside each tile, we rebuild P from Q, K and the logsumexp, then dS is P times dP minus D.
dQ and dK fall out as two more matmuls. Memory stays linear in N, and the backward never stored P.

dO arrow entering, dV = P^T dO block equation highlights.
dP = dO V^T appears as an N x N tile; a full-row bracket with a question mark.
Equation sum_k P_ik dP_ik written; terms animate.
Algebra regroups visually: P (dO V^T) -> dO (P V)^T -> dO * O, with O box glowing.
Column vector D computed from elementwise product of dO and O, then row-summed.
Tile: P recomputed via exp(S - L), then dS = P * (dP - D) heatmap.
dQ = dS K and dK = dS^T Q blocks; memory meter flat while N increases.
short: The MATH beat where sum P*dP becomes rowsum(dO*O). Caption: 'The algebra trick inside FlashAttention's backward.'

A float64 reference passes torch.autograd.gradcheck, and the Triton gradients are within 2x of SDPA's own fp16 error. feather-attn (P1) now trains.

hook: FlashAttention 2 doubled FA1's speed without changing the math. FlashAttention 3 gets about 75% of an H100. Both are about scheduling.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — FlashAttention 2 doubled FA1's speed without changing the math. FlashAttention 3 gets about 75 percent of an H100. Both are about scheduling.

0:15 QUESTION — Your kernel already matches the FA1 algorithm. So what did Tri Dao change in FA2, and what did Shah et al. change for Hopper in FA3? We map each idea to a line in the kernel you wrote.

1:00 INTUITION — FA1 is a correct recipe. FA2 rearranges the kitchen so fewer cooks wait on each other. FA3 hires a dedicated person to fetch ingredients while the chefs never stop chopping. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — FA2 change 1, fewer non-matmul FLOPs: keep O unnormalized and divide by l once at the end; store only L = m + log l. On A100, matmul FLOPs are about 16x cheaper than non-matmul FLOPs (312 TFLOPs tensor vs 19.5 TFLOPs fp32), so every exp and rescale matters. Change 2, parallelism: also parallelize over sequence blocks, not just batch times heads, so long-sequence small-batch runs fill all SMs. Change 3, work partitioning: loop order Q-outer, K-inner, and split warps across Q rows, not across K, so warps never need to exchange partial sums through shared memory. Published: about 2x over FA1, 50 to 73 percent of A100 peak, up to 225 TFLOPs/s training. FA3 on H100: producer-consumer warp specialization with TMA doing async loads; WGMMA async tensor-core instructions; ping-pong scheduling so one warpgroup's softmax overlaps another's GEMM; intra-warpgroup pipelining; FP8 with block quantization and incoherent processing (Hadamard rotation) to tame outliers. Published: up to 740 TFLOPs/s FP16, about 75 percent, and close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8 with 2.6x lower error than baseline FP8.

6:30 CODE — A diff walkthrough, not a new kernel. In your _attn_fwd: point to the deferred acc / l line (FA2 change 1), the grid dimension over Q blocks (change 2), the single-warpgroup Q tile ownership (change 3). Then an annotated pseudo-kernel for FA3: producer warp issues TMA loads of K_j, V_j into a circular shared-memory buffer; consumer warpgroups wait on a barrier, issue async WGMMA for S, compute softmax on the previous tile while the next WGMMA runs. Write it as comments in fa_versions.py, with a table mapping idea, hardware feature, line number.

9:00 RECEIPT — Measure the FA2 claim yourself: time your kernel with the final-normalization trick vs a variant that rescales by l every iteration (FA1 style), same block sizes, fp16, N=4096 on the 4090. Report the speedup. Then compare to the published FA2 vs FA1 number and explain why yours is smaller (Triton already does some of the warp partitioning for you).
10:30 MEASURE — Bar chart: FA1-style variant, FA2-style variant, SDPA, all in TFLOPs/s at N in {1k, 4k, 16k}. Side panel: published FA3 numbers on H100, labeled as published, not measured.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — FA2 cut non-matmul work and fixed parallelism and warp partitioning; FA3 overlaps everything with Hopper's async TMA and WGMMA. Interview line: after the algorithm is IO-optimal, the remaining wins come from keeping tensor cores busy, which means fewer non-matmul FLOPs and overlapping softmax with matmul.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Benchmark: naive vs yours vs SDPA, plus Flash-Decoding.
key_math: A100: 312 TFLOPs (FP16 tensor) vs 19.5 TFLOPs (FP32 non-matmul), ~16x; FA2: O_acc unnormalized, O = O_acc / l at the end; FA3: up to 740 TFLOPs/s FP16 (~75% H100), ~1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8
code_task: fa_versions.py: two variants of your Triton forward (fa1_style with per-iteration normalization, fa2_style with deferred normalization), a benchmark comparing them, and an annotated FA3 producer/consumer pseudo-kernel with an idea-to-line mapping table.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(fa1_style(q,k,v), fa2_style(q,k,v), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) and measured speedup fa2_style vs fa1_style at N=4096 fp16 reported next to the published FA2 ~2x over FA1 figure, with the gap explained.
gotchas: Comparing TFLOPs across GPUs without normalizing to each GPU's peak; reading FA3 numbers as reproducible on a 4090, it needs Hopper TMA and WGMMA; benchmarking variants with different autotuned block sizes, which confounds the algorithm change with tiling.
interview_q: What did FlashAttention-2 change relative to FlashAttention-1? It reduced non-matmul FLOPs by deferring normalization, parallelized over the sequence dimension to fill SMs at small batch sizes, and partitioned work across warps by query rows to avoid shared-memory communication, roughly doubling throughput with identical math.
explainer: Here are three kernels doing identical math. FlashAttention one, two and three. Their speeds are not identical.
On an A100, tensor cores do matmuls about sixteen times faster than ordinary math. So every exp and divide is costly.
FlashAttention two stops normalizing every step. It divides by the sum once at the very end.
It also splits long sequences across more thread blocks, so a batch of one still fills every SM.
And inside a block, each warp owns its own query rows. No warp waits for another to share partial sums.
FlashAttention three targets Hopper. One warp just fetches data with TMA, the hardware copy engine.
Other warpgroups ping pong. While one runs softmax, the other runs a matmul. The tensor cores never idle.
With FP8 and a Hadamard rotation to tame outliers, it reaches about 1.2 petaflops on one H100.

Two bars: tensor core 312 TFLOPs, CUDA core 19.5 TFLOPs; 16x annotation.
Loop timeline: FA1 has a divide in every iteration, FA2 only one at the end.
SM grid mostly empty for FA1 at batch 1, filled for FA2 after sequence-parallel split.
Four warps in a block; FA1 arrows between warps through shared memory, FA2 no arrows.

Gantt chart: two warpgroups alternating GEMM and softmax blocks, tensor core lane continuously busy.
Histogram of activations with outliers, Hadamard rotation flattens it, FP8 grid overlay; 1.2 PFLOPs label.

hook: At decode time, FlashAttention uses a tiny fraction of the GPU. Splitting the KV cache across blocks fixes it. That is Flash-Decoding.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — At decode time, FlashAttention uses a tiny fraction of the GPU. Splitting the KV cache across blocks fixes it. That is Flash-Decoding.

0:15 QUESTION — Time to put numbers on everything: naive, your Triton kernel, SDPA, across sequence lengths, forward and backward. Then the decode case, one query against a long KV cache, where the FlashAttention grid has almost nothing to parallelize. This is the benchmark section of P1, feather-attn.

1:00 INTUITION — During decode there is one query row per sequence. With batch 1 and 32 heads, the forward grid has 32 programs for a GPU with 128 SMs. Most of the chip idles. Flash-Decoding splits the KV sequence into chunks, has many programs each attend to a chunk, then merges results with the online-softmax merge. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Split KV into S chunks. Chunk s gives partial output o_s (normalized within the chunk) and lse_s. Merge: lse = log sum_s exp(lse_s), o = sum_s exp(lse_s - lse) o_s. This is exactly the block merge from the online softmax episode, applied across programs instead of within one. Parallelism goes from B*H to B*H*S programs. Published: up to 8x faster decoding at very long sequences on CodeLlama-34B. Decode is memory-bound: bytes read = 2 * N * H_kv * d * bytes, so the speed ceiling is KV bytes over HBM bandwidth.

5:00 CODE — bench.py: for N in [512, 1k, 2k, 4k, 8k, 16k], causal fwd and fwd+bwd, fp16, d=128, B*H fixed at 32, do_bench naive, flash_fwd, F.scaled_dot_product_attention; save a CSV and plot TFLOPs/s. Then flash_decode(q, k_cache, v_cache, num_splits): q (B,H,1,d), cache (B,H_kv,N,d). Kernel 1 _decode_partial with grid (B*H, num_splits) writes o_part (B,H,S,d) and lse_part (B,H,S). Kernel 2 _decode_reduce merges. Pick num_splits so B*H*S is at least 2x the SM count.

8:30 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(flash_decode(q,k,v,num_splits=s), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) for s in {1, 4, 16, 64}, N up to 128k. Compute achieved HBM bandwidth = KV bytes / time and compare to the 4090's ~1008 GB/s spec; good decode kernels reach a large fraction of it.

10:30 MEASURE — Chart 1: TFLOPs/s vs N for prefill and training, three lines plus percent-of-SDPA labels. Chart 2: decode latency vs KV length, num_splits=1 vs tuned splits, plus achieved GB/s. This chart goes in the feather-attn README.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Prefill is compute-bound so you count TFLOPs; decode is memory-bound so you count GB/s, and you need split-KV to fill the GPU. Interview line: Flash-Decoding parallelizes over the KV length and merges partial softmaxes with their logsumexps, which matters when batch times heads is smaller than the SM count.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Inside Llama 3 and Qwen 3.
key_math: lse = log sum_s e^{lse_s}; o = sum_s e^{lse_s - lse} o_s; decode bytes = 2 N H_kv d * bytes_per_elem; ceiling time = bytes / HBM_BW; programs: B*H -> B*H*S
code_task: bench.py sweep producing CSV + TFLOPs/s plot for naive, flash_fwd, SDPA (fwd and fwd+bwd); flash_decode(q (B,H,1,d), k_cache, v_cache (B,H_kv,N,d), num_splits) with _decode_partial (grid B*H x S) and _decode_reduce kernels.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(flash_decode(q,k,v,num_splits=s), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) for s in {1,4,16,64}; achieved GB/s reported against the 4090's ~1008 GB/s peak.
gotchas: Reporting TFLOPs for decode, where the honest metric is bandwidth; merging partials with plain averaging instead of logsumexp weights; empty chunks when N is not divisible by num_splits produce lse = -inf and nan unless masked.
interview_q: Why is decode attention slow with a standard FlashAttention kernel, and how does Flash-Decoding fix it? With one query per sequence the grid has only batch times heads programs, too few to fill the GPU, and it is memory-bound; Flash-Decoding splits the KV cache into chunks processed in parallel, then combines partial outputs weighted by their logsumexps.
explainer: Here is prefill. Thousands of query rows, plenty of tiles, every SM on the GPU has work.
Now decode. One new token, one query row per head. The grid shrinks to a thin column of programs.
With batch one and thirty two heads, only thirty two of the GPU's SMs light up. The rest sit dark.
Flash decoding cuts the long KV cache into chunks. Each chunk gets its own program.
Now every SM has a chunk. Each returns a partial output and its own log sum exp.
A tiny second kernel merges the partials, weighting each by e to its log sum exp minus the total.
It is the same merge rule as online softmax, just across programs instead of inside one.
On the chart, latency now tracks KV bytes divided by memory bandwidth. That is the ceiling.

Single query row vs long KV cache bar; program grid collapses to one column.
SM grid with 32 lit, 96 dark; utilization meter at 25%.
KV cache bar chopped into 16 colored chunks, each mapped to a program.
SM grid fully lit; each chunk emits (o_s, lse_s) pair.
Reduce kernel funnel combining pairs with weights exp(lse_s - lse).
Side-by-side: online softmax merge formula and the reduce formula, identical.
Latency vs KV length plot with a dashed bandwidth ceiling line; tuned splits hugging it.
